arXiv:2510.02577v1 [math-ph] 02 Oct 2025

Surface Wave Solutions in 1D and 2D for the Broer-Kaup-Boussinesq-Kupershmidt (BKBK) System

Darryl D. Holm,   Ruiao Hu and Hanchun Wang1. Department of Mathematics, Imperial College London,London SW7 2AZ, UK2. DAMTP, University of Cambridge Note: Corresponding author. Email: d.holm@imperial.ac.uk, ORCID ID: 0000-0001-6362-9912 Note: Email: ruiao.hu15@imperial.ac.uk, ORCID ID: 0000-0002-4843-1737 Note: Email: hanchun.wang21@imperial.ac.uk, ORCID ID: 0000-0002-9669-1322
Abstract

The BKBK system is a singular perturbation of the classical shallow water equations which modifies their transport velocity to depend on wave elevation slope. This modification introduces backward diffusion terms proportional to a real parameter κ\kappa. These terms also make BKBK completely integrable as a Hamiltonian system. Remarkably, when κ=i/2\kappa=i/2 the BKBK system may be transformed into the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS). Thus, the BKBK system with its real parameter κ\kappa is complementary to the traditional modulational approach for water waves. We investigate the Lie algebraic and variational properties of the BKBK system in this paper and we study its solution behaviour in certain computational simulations of regularised versions of the 1D and 2D BKBK systems.

In memoriam D.J. Kaup (1939-2022) and B.A. Kupershmidt (1946-2010)

1 Introduction

1.1 BKBK system in one dimension (1D)

The classical shallow water equations in one dimension (1D) for fluid velocity u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) and depth η=η⁡(x,t)\eta=\eta(x,t) on the real line x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} are given by

ut+u​ux+1F​r2​ηx=0,ηt+(u​η)x=0,\displaystyle\begin{split}u_{t}+uu_{x}+\frac{1}{Fr^{2}}\eta_{x}&=0\,,\\ \eta_{t}+(u\eta)_{x}&=0\,,\end{split} (1.1)

in which subscripts in tt and xx denote partial derivatives, F​r2=u02/g​η0Fr^{2}=u_{0}^{2}/g\eta_{0} is the dimension-free Froude number, in which gg is the gravitational constant, u0u_{0} is the mean velocity and η0\eta_{0} is the mean depth for Boussinesq long waves in shallow water. In what follows, we will take F​r=1Fr=1. The dispersion relation ω⁡(k)\omega(k) for linearised wave solutions of the 1D shallow water system in (1.1) proportional to exp⁡(i⁡(k​x−ω​t))\exp(i(kx-\omega t)) with frequency ω\omega and wavenumber kk is then given by

ω2=k2.\omega^{2}=k^{2}. (1.2)

Since the phase velocity ω/k=±1\omega/k=\pm 1 of linearised waves travelling on the real axis is independent of wave number (k)(k), the classical 1D shallow water system (1.1) is said to be dispersionless.

Historically, the shallow water system (1.1) has had a number of interesting dispersive modifications in both 1D and 2D, going back at least to Boussinesq [Bou72]. These modifications are reviewed, e.g., in Broer [Bro75] and Kaup [Kau75], as well as in more recent compendia of references and discussions, such as [CZ24, KS21, KS25].

In this work, we study the following integrable dispersive singular perturbation of the nonlinear long-wave systems in the Boussinesq class,

ut=−(u2/2+η+β​ux)x,ηt=−(u​η+α​ux​x−β​ηx)x,\displaystyle\begin{split}u_{t}&=-\left(u^{2}/2+\eta+\beta u_{x}\right)_{x}\,,\\ \eta_{t}&=-\left(u\eta+\alpha u_{xx}-\beta\eta_{x}\right)_{x}\,,\end{split} (1.3)

with arbitrary constants α\alpha and β\beta. For values α=1/3\alpha=1/3, β=0\beta=0, the system (1.3) was derived by Broer [Bro75] who called it “The oldest, simplest and most widely known set of equations” for dispersive nonlinear long wave propagation. Kupershmidt [Kup85] reduced the number of free parameters in the dispersive nonlinear long-wave system (1.3) by using the invertible change of variables,

u→u,η→η+γux,whereγ:=−β±α+β2,\displaystyle u\to u\,,\ \quad\eta\to\eta+\gamma u_{x}\,,\quad\text{where}\quad\gamma:=-\beta\pm\sqrt{\alpha+\beta^{2}}\,,

to obtain what we call here the Broer-Kaup-Boussinesq-Kupershmidt (BKBK) integrable system,

ut=−(u2/2+η+κ​ux)x=−u​ux−ηx−κ​ux​x,ηt=−(ηv)x=−(ηu)x+κηx​xwithv:=u−κ(lnη)x,κ=±α+β2.\displaystyle\begin{split}{u}_{t}&=-\left({u}^{2}/2+{\eta}+\kappa{u}_{x}\right)_{x}=-uu_{x}-\eta_{x}-\kappa u_{xx}\,,\\ {\eta}_{t}&=-({\eta}v)_{x}=-(\eta u)_{x}+\kappa{\eta}_{xx}\quad\hbox{with}\quad v:=u-\kappa(\ln{\eta})_{x}\,,\\ \kappa&=\pm\sqrt{\alpha+\beta^{2}}\,.\end{split} (1.4)

The real parameter κ\kappa appearing in (1.4) may be regarded as an arbitrary constant, say κ=±1/2\kappa=\pm 1/2, after appropriately rescaling xx and tt. Kupershmidt [Kup85] also found that the system (1.4) for κ=−1/2\kappa=-1/2 possesses three inequivalent compatible Hamiltonian structures and that this tri-Hamiltonian structure implies complete integrability of the system (1.4) for the case κ=−1/2\kappa=-1/2.

However, the backwards diffusion in the motion equation of system (1.4) produces an ill-posed dispersion relation ω2​(k2)\omega^{2}(k^{2}) for the frequency ω\omega as a function of wavenumber kk of the linearised BKBK solutions,

ω2​(k2)=k2​(1−κ2​k2).\omega^{2}(k^{2})=k^{2}(1-\kappa^{2}k^{2})\,. (1.5)

Thus, the BKBK system (1.4) is linearly ill-posed for higher wave numbers, k2>1/κ2k^{2}>1/\kappa^{2}, independently of the sign of the real parameter κ\kappa. Hence, regardless of its complete integrability as a Hamiltonian system for κ=−1/2\kappa=-1/2, the linear ill-posedness of the 1D BKBK system is quite challenging to simulate numerically, since the solutions are linearly unstable for either sign of κ\kappa at higher wave numbers k2>1/κ2k^{2}>1/\kappa^{2}, as discussed in [KS21, KS25].

Plan of the paper. The remainder of the present investigation will proceed as follows.

  • •

    Section 2 discusses the geometric properties of the BKBK system in 1D. We present the various existing Hamiltonian structures of the 1D BKBK system (1.4) and its Euler–Poincaré derivation using symmetry-reduced variational principles [HMR98]. We investigate the Lyapunov stability of 1D BKBK system using the energy–Casimir approach of [HMRW85] and connect the 1D BKBK system to the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation by changing the BKBK dispersion parameter κ\kappa from real to imaginary.

  • •

    Section 3 derives Euler–Poincaré formulation and the Hamiltonian formulation of the BKBK system in two spatial dimensions, as well as its Lie–Poisson bracket, Hamiltonian structures and conservation of potential vorticity (PV).

  • •

    Section 4 derives equilibrium conditions for the BKBK system in two dimensions following the stability results of [HMRW85]. This is done by considering critical points of the sum hΦ​(𝐮,η)=hΦ​(𝐮,η)+CΦh_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u},\eta)=h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u},\eta)+C_{\Phi} of the Hamiltonian found in section 3 plus its Casimir constants of motion, CΦC_{\Phi} in (3.16). By demanding positivity the second variation of HCH_{C} we then derive spectral conditions for linear Lyapunov stability of the corresponding energy-Casimir class of equilibrium solutions of the 2D BKBK system.

  • •

    Section 5 provides computational simulations of the solution behaviour for the BKBK system in both 1D and 2D. Different computational methods are employed for numerically regularising the BKBK systems in 1D and 2D. In 1D, we use a 4t​h4^{th}-order dissipation reminiscent of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation for stability. In 2D, we use a Hamiltonian regularisation where nonlinear dispersions are imposed by introducing an modified Hamiltonian that introduce energy costs for large wave height gradients.

  • •

    Section 6 provides a summary conclusion and outlook for future research.

2 BKBK system in 1D

The 1D dispersive BKBK system in (1.4) possesses three inequivalent compatible Hamiltonian formulations [Kau75, Kup85, CDM24]. One of these is the well-known constant-coefficient Hamiltonian structure for the fluid velocity uu and depth η\eta that is defined through the Poisson bracket {⋅,⋅}c\{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\}_{c}. For arbitrary functions F,GF,G of the variables (u,η)(u,\eta), {⋅,⋅}c\{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\}_{c} is defined by

{F,G}c​(u,η)=∫ℝ[δ​Gδ​η​∂xδ​Fδ​u−δ​Fδ​η​∂xδ​Gδ​u]​𝑑x.\displaystyle\{F,G\}_{c}(u,\eta)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left[\frac{\delta G}{\delta\eta}\partial_{x}\frac{\delta F}{\delta u}-\frac{\delta F}{\delta\eta}\partial_{x}\frac{\delta G}{\delta u}\right]\,dx\,. (2.1)

Being a bilinear, antisymmetric, constant-coefficient differential operator, the Poisson bracket {⋅,⋅}c\{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\}_{c} also satisfies the Jacobi identity,

{A,{B,D}c}c+{B,{D,A}c}c+{D,{A,B}c}c=0,\{A\,,\,\{B\,,\,D\}_{c}\}_{c}+\{B\,,\,\{D\,,\,A\}_{c}\}_{c}+\{D\,,\,\{A\,,\,B\}_{c}\}_{c}=0\,, (2.2)

for arbitrary functionals A,B,DA,B,D of the variables uu and η\eta. The time evolution of an arbitrary functional FF of (u,η)(u,\eta) is generated by the Hamiltonian functional HH on the same variables through the {⋅,⋅}c\{\cdot\,,\,\cdot\}_{c} by

dd​t​F​(u,η)={F,H}c​(u,η),\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}F(u,\eta)=\{F,H\}_{c}(u,\eta)\,, (2.3)

such that the evolution of (u,η)(u,\eta) can be expressed in Poisson operator form as

∂t[uη]=−[0∂x∂x0]​[δ​H/δ​uδ​H/δ​η],\partial_{t}\begin{bmatrix}u\\ \eta\end{bmatrix}=-\begin{bmatrix}0&\partial_{x}\\ \partial_{x}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\delta{H}/\delta u\\ \delta{H}/\delta\eta\end{bmatrix}, (2.4)

with 1D BKBK Hamiltonian H⁡(u,η)H(u,\eta) and variations δ​Hδ​u\frac{\delta H}{\delta u} and δ​Hδ​η\frac{\delta H}{\delta\eta} given by

H⁡(u,η):=∫ℝ12ηu2−κu∂xη+12η2dxsuch thatδ​Hδ​u=ηvwithv:=u−κ∂xlnη,δ​Hδ​η=12u2+η2+κ∂xu.\displaystyle\begin{split}H(u,\eta)&:=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\tfrac{1}{2}\eta u^{2}-\kappa u\partial_{x}\eta+\tfrac{1}{2}\eta^{2}\,dx\quad\text{such that}\\ \frac{\delta H}{\delta u}&=\eta v\quad\hbox{with}\quad v:=u-\kappa\partial_{x}\ln\eta\,,\quad\frac{\delta H}{\delta\eta}=\frac{1}{2}u^{2}+\frac{\eta}{2}+\kappa\partial_{x}u\,.\end{split} (2.5)

The operation of the matrix Poisson operator in (2.4) on the variational derivatives of HH yields the 1D BKBK system (1.4). From the Hamiltonian (2.5), we see that the sign-indefinite terms multiplying κ\kappa correspond to the terms that generate the singular dispersive perturbations of the classical shallow water equations appearing in the BKBK system (1.4).

Remark 2.1.

Equilibrium solutions of the BKBK system (1.4) satisfy,

δ​HC=0,forHC:=H⁡(u,η)+C​∫u​𝑑x=0,\displaystyle\delta H_{C}=0\,,\quad\hbox{for}\quad H_{C}:={H}(u,\eta)+C\int u\,dx=0\,, (2.6)

for an arbitrary constant speed CC. The second variation δ2​HC​(u,η)\delta^{2}{H}_{C}(u,\eta) is the Hamiltonian for the linearised flow in an infinitesimal neighbourhood of an equilibrium solution satisfying δ​HC=0\delta H_{C}=0 [HMRW85]. Consequently, the Lyapunov stability of these BKBK equilibria may be tested by considering whether the following quadratic form δ2​HC​(u,η)\delta^{2}{H}_{C}(u,\eta) for the BKBK system is definite in sign when evaluated at an equilibrium solution (ue​(x),ηe​(x))(u_{e}(x),\eta_{e}(x)).

δ2​HC​(u,η)|(ue​(x),ηe​(x))\displaystyle\delta^{2}{H}_{C}(u,\eta)\Big|_{(u_{e}(x),\eta_{e}(x))} =∫ℝ[δ​uδ​η]T​[ηeueue1]​[δ​uδ​η]​𝑑x+2​κ​∫ℝδ​ux​δ​η​𝑑x\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\begin{bmatrix}\delta u\\ \delta\eta\end{bmatrix}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}\eta_{e}&u_{e}\\ u_{e}&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\delta u\\ \delta\eta\end{bmatrix}dx+2\kappa\int_{\mathbb{R}}\delta u_{x}\delta\eta\,dx (2.7)
=∫ℝ[δ​uδ​η]T​[ηeue−κ∂xue+κ∂x1]​[δ​uδ​η]​𝑑x.\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\begin{bmatrix}\delta u\\ \delta\eta\end{bmatrix}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}\eta_{e}&u_{e}-\kappa\partial_{x}\\ u_{e}+\kappa\partial_{x}&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\delta u\\ \delta\eta\end{bmatrix}dx\,. (2.8)

For the case of 1D shallow water dynamics arising for κ=0\kappa=0, definiteness in sign of δ2​HC​(𝐮e,ηe)\delta^{2}H_{C}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e}) provides sufficient conditions for linear Lyapunov stability of shallow water equilibrium solutions that are obtained from setting δ​HC​(𝐮e,ηe)=0\delta H_{C}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e})=0 with κ=0\kappa=0. This was shown for 2D shallow water dynamics in [HMRW83, HMRW85]. However, for non-zero κ\kappa, the linear stability of perturbed 1D BKBK equilibrium solutions in the class δ​HC​(ue,ηe)=0\delta H_{C}({u}_{e},\eta_{e})=0 requires the additional condition that the spectrum of the symmetric elliptic operator in (2.8) must also be positive definite. However, the symbol of the elliptic operator in (2.8) is of the form

σ⁡(k2)=ηe​(x)−(ue2​(x)+κ2​k2),\displaystyle\sigma(k^{2})={\eta}_{e}(x)-\big({u}_{e}^{2}(x)+\kappa^{2}\,k^{2}\big)\,, (2.9)

which cannot remain positive at arbitrarily high wavenumber (k)(k) for non-zero κ\kappa. Hence, the linear Lyapunov stability condition of positivity of the 2nd variation cannot be enforced at arbitrarily high wavenumber, (k)(k). Once high wave numbers were introduced in perturbing 1D BKBK equilibrium solutions such as its travelling wave solution, the equilibrium would no longer be linearly Lyapunov stable and the nonlinear terms would generate even higher wave numbers.

Connection to Nonlinear Schrödinger equation

The 1D BKBK system (1.4) can be expressed in terms of the modified transport velocity vv. In this case, we have

vt=−(v22−κ22(ηxη)2+κ2∂x2ηη+η)x,ηt=−(ηv)x.\displaystyle\begin{split}v_{t}=-\left(\frac{v^{2}}{2}-\frac{\kappa^{2}}{2}\left(\frac{\eta_{x}}{\eta}\right)^{2}+\kappa^{2}\frac{\partial_{x}^{2}\eta}{\eta}+\eta\right)_{x}\,,\quad\eta_{t}=-\,(\eta v)_{x}\,.\end{split} (2.10)

System (2.10) can be expressed using the constant-coefficient Poisson bracket (2.4) in combination with the following modified Hamiltonian 𝔥\mathfrak{h},

𝔥⁡(v,η)=∫ℝ12​η​v2−κ22​η​(∂xη)2+12​η2​𝑑x=∫ℝ12​η​v2−κ2​(∂xη)2+12​η2​𝑑x.\displaystyle\mathfrak{h}(v,\eta)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{1}{2}\eta v^{2}-\frac{\kappa^{2}}{2\eta}(\partial_{x}\eta)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\eta^{2}\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{1}{2}\eta v^{2}-\kappa^{2}(\partial_{x}\sqrt{\eta})^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\eta^{2}\,dx\,. (2.11)

One may notice that the term (∂xη)2(\partial_{x}\sqrt{\eta})^{2} in the second expression for the Hamiltonian here is in the form of the Fisher–Rao metric of η\eta. It has not escaped our attention that the Hamiltonian 𝔥\mathfrak{h} in (2.11) is similar to the Hamiltonian of the Nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation, when expressed in the Madelung variables (ρ,ϕ)(\rho,\phi) related to the complex wave function ψ\psi by ψ=η​exp⁡(i​ϕ)\psi=\sqrt{\eta}\exp(i\phi) and v=∂xϕv=\partial_{x}\phi [Mad27].

Choosing κ=i2\kappa=\frac{i}{2} after transforming variables η​v=Im⁡(ψ∗​∂xψ)\eta v={\rm Im}(\psi^{*}\partial_{x}\psi) and η=‖ψ‖2\eta=\|\psi\|^{2} in the Hamiltonian (2.11) yields the Hamiltonian for the focusing NLS equation with canonical complex variables (ψ,ψ∗)(\psi,\psi^{*}) and Planck constant ℏ\hbar set equal to unity.

Inserting κ=i2\kappa=\frac{i}{2} into the dispersion relation ω2​(k2)\omega^{2}(k^{2}) in (1.5), the dependence of frequency ω\omega on wavenumber kk of the linearised solutions of the BKBK system is modified to

ω2​(k2)=k2​(1+14​k2).\omega^{2}(k^{2})=k^{2}\left(1+\tfrac{1}{4}k^{2}\right)\,. (2.12)

This is a notable observation, since nonlinear modulation instability of water waves has been traditionally using with the focusing NLS equation, [Per83]. Given this observation, studies of instability of water waves using the 1D BKBK system with real-valued κ\kappa may be regarded as being complementary to the study of modulation instability of water waves using the NLS equation.

Lie–Poisson bracket dynamics.

Via an invertible change of variables (u,η)→(m:=η​u,η)(u,\eta)\to(m:=\eta u,\eta) for u≠0u\neq 0, the 1D BKBK system (1.4) may be cast into the following equivalent form

∂tm+∂x(m​v)+m​∂xv+η​∂xℬ=0,∂tη+∂x(v​η)=0,\displaystyle\begin{split}&\partial_{t}m+\partial_{x}\left(mv\right)+m\partial_{x}v+\eta\partial_{x}\mathcal{B}=0\,,\\ &\partial_{t}\eta+\partial_{x}(v\eta)=0\,,\end{split} (2.13)

where the quantities vv and ℬ\mathcal{B} are defined by variations of the Hamiltonian functional (2.5) expressed in the new variables (m,η)(m,\eta), as

h⁡(m,η):=∫ℝm22​η−κ​m​∂x(ln⁡η)+12​η2​dx,such that,v:=δ​hδ​m=u−κ∂xlnη,ℬ:=δ​hδ​η=−|u|22+κη∂x(ηu)+η.\displaystyle\begin{split}h(m,\eta)&:=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{m^{2}}{2\eta}-\kappa m\,\partial_{x}(\ln\eta)+\tfrac{1}{2}\eta^{2}\,dx\,,\quad\text{such that}\,,\\ v&:=\frac{\delta h}{\delta m}=u-\kappa\partial_{x}\ln\eta\,,\quad\mathcal{B}:=\frac{\delta h}{\delta\eta}=-\frac{|u|^{2}}{2}+\frac{\kappa}{\eta}\partial_{x}(\eta u)+\eta\,.\end{split} (2.14)

In fact, system (2.13) takes the form of a Lie–Poisson system on the semidirect product Lie co-algebra 𝔰∗=𝔛∗​(ℝ)⋉Den⁡(ℝ)\mathfrak{s}^{*}=\mathfrak{X}^{*}(\mathbb{R})\ltimes\operatorname{Den}(\mathbb{R}) [HK83, HMR98, Hol25]. In the Lie–Poisson formulation, one identifies mm as the scalar coefficient part of the momentum 11-form density m~:=m​d​x⊗d​x∈𝔛∗​(ℝ)\widetilde{m}:=m\,dx\otimes dx\in\mathfrak{X}^{*}(\mathbb{R}) and η\eta as the scalar coefficient part of the density η~=η​d​x∈Den⁡(ℝ)\widetilde{\eta}=\eta\,dx\in\operatorname{Den}(\mathbb{R}). On the Lie co-algebra of the Lie algebra 𝔰=𝔛⁡(ℝ)⋉Den⁡(ℝ)\mathfrak{s}=\mathfrak{X}(\mathbb{R})\ltimes\operatorname{Den}(\mathbb{R}), the Lie–Poisson bracket {⋅,⋅}\{\cdot,\cdot\} may be defined in terms of the basis coefficients, for arbitrary f,gf,g functionals of (m,η)(m,\eta), as

{f,g}​(m,η):=∫ℝm⁡(δ​fδ​m​∂xδ​gδ​m−δ​gδ​m​∂xδ​fδ​m)+η⁡(δ​fδ​m​∂xδ​gδ​η−δ​gδ​m​∂xδ​fδ​η)​𝑑x.\displaystyle\begin{split}\{f,g\}(m,\eta)&:=\int_{\mathbb{R}}m\left(\frac{\delta f}{\delta m}\partial_{x}\frac{\delta g}{\delta m}-\frac{\delta g}{\delta m}\partial_{x}\frac{\delta f}{\delta m}\right)+\eta\left(\frac{\delta f}{\delta m}\partial_{x}\frac{\delta g}{\delta\eta}-\frac{\delta g}{\delta m}\partial_{x}\frac{\delta f}{\delta\eta}\right)\,dx\,.\end{split} (2.15)

Thus, the 1D BKBK system (2.13) can be expressed in Lie–Poisson operator form as

∂t[mη]=−[∂xm+m∂xη∂x∂xη0]​[δ​h/δ​mδ​h/δ​η]=−[∂x(m​δ​hδ​m)+m​∂xδ​hδ​m+η​∂xδ​hδ​η∂x(η​δ​hδ​m)].\partial_{t}\begin{bmatrix}m\\ \eta\end{bmatrix}=-\begin{bmatrix}\partial_{x}m+m\partial_{x}&\eta\partial_{x}\\ \partial_{x}\eta&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\delta h/\delta m\\ \delta h/\delta\eta\end{bmatrix}=-\begin{bmatrix}\partial_{x}\left(m\frac{\delta h}{\delta m}\right)+m\partial_{x}\frac{\delta h}{\delta m}+\eta\partial_{x}\frac{\delta h}{\delta\eta}\\ \partial_{x}\big(\eta\tfrac{\delta h}{\delta m}\big)\end{bmatrix}. (2.16)

Here, the spatial partial derivatives appearing in the Poisson matrix of (2.16) each act on all terms to their right arising after after performing the matrix vector multiplication. For background in the derivation and applications of semidirect-product Lie–Poisson brackets for continuum models, see, e.g., [HK83, HMR98, Hol25].

Having expressed the BKBK system in the Lie–Poisson form in equation (2.16), one sees that the ‘dispersive term’ proportional to the constant κ\kappa, modifies the transport velocity (δ​h/δ​m\delta h/\delta m) from uu in the classical shallow water case to δ​h/δ​m=v:=u−κ​∂xln⁡η\delta h/\delta m=v:=u-\kappa\partial_{x}\ln\eta in the dynamics for both depth η\eta and momentum density mm.

The equivalent Euler–Poincaré derivation.

The Lie–Poisson Hamiltonian form of the BKBK system has an equivalent Euler–Poincaré Lagrangian form arising from the corresponding Hamilton variational principle. Namely, the 1D BKBK system (1.4) can be derived from an Euler–Poincaré variational principle [HMR98] with advected quantity η\eta given by,

0=δ​S=δ​∫t0t1ℓ⁡(v,η)​𝑑t=δ​∫t0t1∫ℝ12​η​|v+κ​∂xln⁡η|2−12​η2​𝑑x​𝑑t,\displaystyle 0=\delta S=\delta\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\ell(v,\eta)\,dt=\delta\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{1}{2}\eta|v+\kappa\partial_{x}\ln\eta|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\eta^{2}\,dx\,dt\,, (2.17)

with constrained variations given by

δv=∂tw−w∂xv+v∂xwandδη=−∂x(wη).\displaystyle\delta v=\partial_{t}w-w\partial_{x}v+v\partial_{x}w\quad\hbox{and}\quad\delta\eta=-\partial_{x}(w\eta)\,. (2.18)

Here, ww is an arbitrary vector field that vanishes on the temporal endpoints and obeys appropriate decay conditions as |x|→∞|x|\rightarrow\infty. After taking these constrained variations and integrating by parts in space and time the Euler–Poincaré formulation with Lagrangian (2.17) recovers the 1D BKBK system in (1.4). For the intrinsic expression of the Euler–Poincaré and Lie–Poisson formulation of the BKBK system in terms of actions of the diffeomorphism group, see, e.g., [HMR98].

A virtue of having derived the 1D BKBK system (1.4) via an Euler–Poincaré variational principle with advected quantities is that the definition of its Lagrangian extends easily to any number of spatial dimensions. In particular, one may derive the 2D BKBK system from the same variational principle, as shown in section 4. As we will see, equivalence of the Euler–Poincaré variational principle and the Lie–Poisson Hamiltonian structure implies that the 2D BKBK system also satisfies the semidirect-product Lie–Poisson bracket formulation that appears naturally in the ideal dynamics of all continuum models. Moreover, the Madelung transform of the 1D BKBK system for κ=i/2\kappa=i/2 to the focusing NLS equation also applies for the 2D BKBK system, but only in the case of potential flow,

𝐮=∇ϕ=𝐯+κ∇lnη.\displaystyle\mathbf{u}=\nabla\phi=\mathbf{v}+\kappa\nabla\ln\eta\,. (2.19)

3 BKBK system in 2D

This section extends the geometric structures of the 1D BKBK system to 2D. In particular, the Euler–Poincaré derivations of the 2D BKBK system, as well as its Hamiltonian structures and their implications such as the existence of potential vorticity and its associated conservation laws as presented.

Variational principles of 2D BKBK.

To extend the 1D BKBK system (1.4) defined on the real line to the 2D plane, we denote by 𝐮=𝐮⁡(𝐱,t)\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x},t) for the fluid velocity and η=η⁡(𝐱,t)\eta=\eta(\mathbf{x},t) for the fluid depth where 𝐱∈ℝ2\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. Geometrically, we have the fluid velocity vector field u=𝐮⋅∇∈𝔛(ℝ2)u=\mathbf{u}\cdot\,\nabla\in\mathfrak{X}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) and the fluid depth as the density η~=η​d2​x∈Den⁡(ℝ2)\widetilde{\eta}=\eta\,d^{2}x\in\operatorname{Den}(\mathbb{R}^{2}). The BKBK modified transport velocity vector field is defined to be,

𝐯:=𝐮−κ∇lnη.\displaystyle\mathbf{v}:=\mathbf{u}-\kappa\nabla\ln\eta\,. (3.1)

We postulate that the dynamics of 𝐮\mathbf{u} and η\eta are obtained from the following Euler–Poincaré variational principle with advected quantity,

0=δS[𝐯,η]=δ∫t0t1ℓ(𝐯,η)dt=δ∫t0t1∫ℝ212η|𝐯+κ∇lnη|2−12η2d2xdt,\displaystyle 0=\delta S[\mathbf{v},\eta]=\delta\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\ell(\mathbf{v},\eta)\,dt=\delta\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\frac{1}{2}\eta|\mathbf{v}+\kappa\nabla\ln\eta|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\eta^{2}\,d^{2}x\,dt\,, (3.2)

with constrained variations δ​𝐯=∂t𝐰−[𝐰,𝐯]\delta\mathbf{v}=\partial_{t}{\mathbf{w}}-[{\mathbf{w}},\mathbf{v}] and δη=−∇⋅(𝐰η)\delta\eta=-\nabla\cdot({\mathbf{w}}\eta), where 𝐰{\mathbf{w}} is an arbitrary vector that vanish on temporal boundaries and appropriate decay conditions as x→∞x\rightarrow\infty. Here, [⋅,⋅][\cdot,\cdot] is the Jacobi–Lie bracket of vector fields, [𝐰,𝐯]=𝐰⋅∇𝐯−𝐯⋅∇𝐰[{\mathbf{w}},\mathbf{v}]={\mathbf{w}}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla{\mathbf{w}}. Applying the Euler–Poincaré theorem [HMR98], the resulting Euler–Poincaré equation and the advection equation of η\eta form the 2D BKBK system

∂t𝐮+𝐯⋅∇𝐮+ui∇vi=∇ℬ,∂tη+div⁡(η​𝐯)=0,where𝐯=𝐮−κ∇lnη,ℬ:=(12|u|2−κηdiv(η𝐮)−η).\displaystyle\begin{split}&\partial_{t}\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{u}+u_{i}\nabla v^{i}=\nabla{\cal B}\,,\\ &\partial_{t}\eta+\operatorname{div}(\eta\mathbf{v})=0\,,\\ &\text{where}\quad\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}-\kappa\nabla\ln\eta\,,\quad{\cal B}:=\left(\frac{1}{2}|u|^{2}-\frac{\kappa}{\eta}\operatorname{div}\left(\eta\mathbf{u}\right)-\eta\right)\,.\end{split} (3.3)

In the 2D BKBK system (3.3), one sees that the term in the Lagrangian functional (3.2) proportional to κ\kappa plays two roles. First, it serves to add the standard dispersion term for shallow water waves, −κη−1∇div(η𝐮)-\kappa\eta^{-1}\nabla\operatorname{div}(\eta\mathbf{u}). Second, it serves to enhance the shallow water fluid transport velocity 𝐮\mathbf{u} by an added transport velocity, −κ∇lnη-\kappa\nabla\ln\eta, which involves the gradient of the wave elevation.

By a direct calculation, the 2D BKBK system in (3.3) implies the following Kelvin theorem

dd​t​∮c⁡(v)𝐮⋅𝑑𝐱=∮c⁡(v)(∂t𝐮−𝐯×curl​𝐮)⋅𝑑𝐱=∮c⁡(v)∇ℬ~⋅𝑑𝐱=0,\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\oint_{c(v)}\mathbf{u}\cdot d\mathbf{x}=\oint_{c(v)}\big(\partial_{t}\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\times{\rm curl}\mathbf{u}\big)\cdot d\mathbf{x}=\oint_{c(v)}\nabla\tilde{\cal B}\cdot d\mathbf{x}=0\,, (3.4)

where c⁡(v)c(v) is a material loop moving with the BKBK modified transport velocity vector field 𝐯\mathbf{v}.

Remark 3.1.

The definition 𝐯=𝐮−κ∇lnη\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}-\kappa\nabla\ln\eta implies a constrained variation for 𝐮\mathbf{u} arising from the constrained variations of 𝐯\mathbf{v} and η\eta. In particular,

δ𝐮=δ𝐯+κ∇(1ηδη)=∂t𝐰−[𝐰,𝐯]−κ∇(1η∇⋅(𝐰η))=∂t𝐰−[𝐰,𝐮−κ∇lnη]−κ∇(1η∇⋅(𝐰η)).\displaystyle\begin{split}\delta\mathbf{u}=\delta\mathbf{v}+\kappa\nabla\left(\frac{1}{\eta}\delta\eta\right)&=\partial_{t}{\mathbf{w}}-[{\mathbf{w}},\mathbf{v}]-\kappa\nabla\left(\frac{1}{\eta}\nabla\cdot({\mathbf{w}}\eta)\right)\\ &=\partial_{t}{\mathbf{w}}-\ [{\mathbf{w}},\mathbf{u}-\kappa\nabla\ln\eta]-\kappa\nabla\left(\frac{1}{\eta}\nabla\cdot({\mathbf{w}}\eta)\right)\,.\end{split} (3.5)

Expressing the action principle (3.2) in terms of (𝐮,η)(\mathbf{u},\eta) and imposing the constrained variations for η\eta and 𝐮\mathbf{u} as presented above yield the 2D BKBK system (3.3).

Remark 3.2.

One may express the 2D BKBK system (3.3) in the variables (𝐯,η)(\mathbf{v},\eta) as

∂t𝐯+𝐯⋅∇𝐯+vi∇vi=∇ℬ^,whereℬ^=|𝐯|22+κ22|∇lnη|2−κ2η△η−η,∂tη+∇⋅(𝐯​η)=0.\displaystyle\begin{split}&\partial_{t}\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{v}+v_{i}\nabla v^{i}=\nabla\widehat{\mathcal{B}}\,,\quad\text{where}\quad\widehat{\cal{B}}=\frac{|\mathbf{v}|^{2}}{2}+\frac{\kappa^{2}}{2}|\nabla\ln\eta|^{2}-\frac{\kappa^{2}}{\eta}\triangle\eta-\eta\,,\\ &\partial_{t}\eta+\nabla\cdot\left(\mathbf{v}\eta\right)=0\,.\end{split} (3.6)

The Kelvin circulation dynamics for the transport velocity 𝐯\mathbf{v} has the same form as for the fluid velocity 𝐮\mathbf{u}. Let c⁡(v)c(v) be the material loop moving with the vector field 𝐯\mathbf{v},

dd​t​∮c⁡(v)𝐯⋅𝑑𝐱=∮c⁡(v)∇ℬ^⋅𝑑𝐱=0.\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\oint_{c(v)}\mathbf{v}\cdot d\mathbf{x}=\oint_{c(v)}\nabla\widehat{\cal B}\cdot d\mathbf{x}=0\,. (3.7)

Hamiltonian structures for 2D BKBK.

In generalising the semidirect-product Lie–Poisson bracket in equation (2.15) from one spatial dimension to two spatial dimensions, the Lie–Poisson Hamiltonian formulation of the 1D BKBK system in (2.16) generalises to the following 2D BKBK system in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} index notation:

∂t[miη]=−[∂jmi+mj∂iη∂i∂jη0]​[δ​h/δ​mjδ​h/δ​η],\partial_{t}\begin{bmatrix}m_{i}\\ \eta\end{bmatrix}=-\begin{bmatrix}\partial_{j}m_{i}+m_{j}\partial_{i}&\eta\partial_{i}\\ \partial_{j}\eta&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\delta h/\delta m_{j}\\ \delta h/\delta\eta\end{bmatrix}, (3.8)

with i,j=1,2i,j=1,2 and standard Einstein summation notation. Its Hamiltonian functional is written in the variables (𝐦,η)(\mathbf{m},\eta) as

h⁡(𝐦,η):=∫ℝ|𝐦|22​η−κ​𝐦⋅∇(ln⁡η)+12​η2​d2​x,such thatδ​hδ​𝐦=𝐮−κ∇lnη=𝐯,δ​hδ​η=−|𝐮|22+η+κη∇⋅(η𝐮)=−ℬ.\displaystyle\begin{split}h(\mathbf{m},\eta)&:=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{|\mathbf{m}|^{2}}{2\eta}-\kappa\mathbf{m}\cdot\nabla(\ln\eta)+\frac{1}{2}\eta^{2}\,d^{2}x\,,\quad\text{such that}\\ \frac{\delta h}{\delta\mathbf{m}}&=\mathbf{u}-\kappa\nabla\ln\eta=\mathbf{v}\,,\quad\frac{\delta h}{\delta\eta}=-\frac{|\mathbf{u}|^{2}}{2}+\eta+\frac{\kappa}{\eta}\nabla\cdot(\eta\mathbf{u})=-{\cal B}\,.\end{split} (3.9)

One may directly calculate the inverse transformation of variables (𝐦,η)→(𝐮=𝐦/η,η)(\mathbf{m},\eta)\to(\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{m}/\eta,\eta) for the 2D version of the Lie–Poisson structure in (3.8) and thereby determine the equations of motion in the standard shallow water variables (𝐮,η)(\mathbf{u},\eta). In this case, the Poisson matrix operated may be computed as follows

[δk​i/η−mk/η201]​[∂jmi+mj∂iη∂i∂jη0]​[δj​l/η0−ml/η21]=[(uk,l−ul,k)/η∂k∂l0].\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}\delta_{ki}/\eta&-m_{k}/\eta^{2}\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\partial_{j}m_{i}+m_{j}\partial_{i}&\eta\partial_{i}\\ \partial_{j}\eta&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\delta_{jl}/\eta&0\\ -m_{l}/\eta^{2}&1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}(u_{k,l}-u_{l,k})/\eta&\partial_{k}\\ \partial_{l}&0\end{bmatrix}\,. (3.10)

Let q∈ℱ⁡(ℝ2)q\in\mathcal{F}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) be the scalar potential vorticity (PV) defined by

q:=1η​𝐳^⋅curl⁡𝐮=1η​(∂xu2−∂yu1).\displaystyle q:=\frac{1}{\eta}\mathbf{\widehat{z}}\cdot\operatorname{curl}\mathbf{u}=\frac{1}{\eta}(\partial_{x}u_{2}-\partial_{y}u_{1})\,. (3.11)

For notational convenience, the 2D velocity 𝐮\mathbf{u} in (3.11) is written as a three dimensional vector 𝐮=(u1,u2,0)\mathbf{u}=(u_{1},u_{2},0) and the function qq for PV is written as a vertical component 𝐪:=q​𝐳^\mathbf{q}:=q\mathbf{\widehat{z}}, so that 𝐪×𝐮\mathbf{q}\times\mathbf{u} rotates a horizontal vector 𝐮\mathbf{u} clockwise by π/2\pi/2. The transformed Poisson matrix in (3.10) yields the following Poisson bracket

{F,H}(𝐮,η)=∫ℝ[−δ​Fδ​𝐮⋅qδ​Hδ​𝐮T+δ​Gδ​η∇⋅δ​Fδ​𝐮−δ​Fδ​η∇⋅δ​Gδ​𝐮]dx.\displaystyle\{F,H\}(\mathbf{u},\eta)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left[-\frac{\delta F}{\delta\mathbf{u}}\cdot q\frac{\delta H}{\delta\mathbf{u}}^{T}+\frac{\delta G}{\delta\eta}\nabla\cdot\frac{\delta F}{\delta\mathbf{u}}-\frac{\delta F}{\delta\eta}\nabla\cdot\frac{\delta G}{\delta\mathbf{u}}\right]\,dx\,. (3.12)

Here, the superscript (⋅)T(\cdot)^{T} is defined for two dimensional vectors as (u1,u2)T:=(−u2,u1)(u_{1},u_{2})^{T}:=(-u_{2},u_{1}). Consequently, the 2D BKBK system (3.3) may be expressed with a Poisson operator (3.10) involving the potential vorticity qq in the vector form 𝐪:=q​𝐳^\mathbf{q}:=q\mathbf{\widehat{z}} as

∂t[𝐮η]=−[𝐪×∇∇⁣⋅0]​[δ​h~/δ​𝐮=η​𝐯δ​h~/δ​η=ℬ~],\displaystyle\begin{split}\partial_{t}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{u}\\ \eta\end{bmatrix}&=-\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{q}\times&\nabla\\ \nabla\cdot&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\delta\tilde{h}/\delta\mathbf{u}=\eta\mathbf{v}\\ \delta\tilde{h}/\delta\eta=\tilde{\cal B}\end{bmatrix}\,,\end{split} (3.13)

for Hamiltonian (3.9) written in the variables (𝐮,η)(\mathbf{u},\eta) as

h~​(𝐮,η):=∫Mη​|𝐮|22−κ​𝐮⋅∇η+12​η2​d2​x,such thatδ​h~δ​u=η𝐮−κ∇η=η𝐯,δ​h~δ​η=12|𝐮|2+κdiv(𝐮)+η=:ℬ~(𝐮,η).\displaystyle\begin{split}\widetilde{h}(\mathbf{u},\eta)&:=\int_{M}\eta\frac{|\mathbf{u}|^{2}}{2}-\kappa\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\eta+\frac{1}{2}\eta^{2}\,d^{2}x\,,\quad\text{such that}\\ \frac{\delta\widetilde{h}}{\delta u}&=\eta\mathbf{u}-\kappa\nabla\eta=\eta\mathbf{v}\,,\quad\frac{\delta\widetilde{h}}{\delta\eta}=\frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{u}|^{2}+\kappa\,{\rm div}(\mathbf{u})+\eta=:\tilde{\cal B}(\mathbf{u},\eta)\,.\end{split} (3.14)

The PV scalar function qq satisfies an advection equation which may be readily obtained by taking the curl\operatorname{curl} of the 𝐮\mathbf{u} equation in (3.3)

(∂t+𝐯⋅∇)q=(∂t+(𝐮−κ∇lnη)⋅∇)q=0.\displaystyle\Big(\partial_{t}+\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla\Big)q=\Big(\partial_{t}+(\mathbf{u}-\kappa\nabla\ln\eta)\cdot\nabla\Big)q=0\,. (3.15)

In turn, the PV advection equation (3.15) implies conservation by the 2D BKBK equations in (3.13) of the quantity

CΦ:=∫ℝ2η​Φ​(q)​d2​x,\displaystyle C_{\Phi}:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\eta\Phi(q)\,d^{2}x\,, (3.16)

for any differentiable function Φ\Phi. It is clear that the functional CΦC_{\Phi} is conserved for any differentiable function Φ\Phi, since the depth η\eta and the potential vorticity qq are both advected quantities. Moreover, the variational derivative of the functional CΦC_{\Phi} comprises a null eigenvector of the Lie–Poisson operator in terms of variables (m,η)(m,\eta) in equation (3.8). Consequently, the functionals CΦC_{\Phi} in (3.16) for the Lie–Poisson formulation of the 2D BKBK system would in fact be conserved for any Hamiltonian depending on the variables (m,η)(m,\eta).

4 Stability of equilibrium solutions of the 2D BKBK system

This section derives equilibrium conditions for the 2D BKBK system following the nonlinear stability analysis of [HMRW85]. This is done in two stages. First, we consider the critical points of the sum hΦ​(𝐮,η):=h⁡(𝐮,η)+CΦh_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u},\eta):=h(\mathbf{u},\eta)+C_{\Phi} of the Hamiltonian found in section 3 plus its Casimir constants of motion, CΦC_{\Phi} in (3.16). Then, by demanding positivity of the second variation of hΦ​(𝐮,η)h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u},\eta), we derive spectral conditions for linear Lyapunov stability of the corresponding energy-Casimir class of equilibrium solutions of the 2D BKBK system.

Let (𝐮e,ηe,qe)(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e},q_{e}) be an equilibrium solution to the 2D BKBK system in (3.3) augmented with the advection equation of scalar PV, denoted as qq. We denote the equilibrium transport velocity vector 𝐯e\mathbf{v}_{e} by 𝐯e=𝐮e−κ∇lnηe\mathbf{v}_{e}=\mathbf{u}_{e}-\kappa\nabla\ln\eta_{e}. The equilibrium solutions satisfy

𝐯e×ωe𝐳^=∇ℬ~(𝐮e,ηe),𝐯e⋅∇qe=0,anddiv(ηe𝐯e)=0.\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{e}\times\omega_{e}\mathbf{\widehat{z}}=\nabla\tilde{\cal B}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e})\,,\quad\mathbf{v}_{e}\cdot\nabla q_{e}=0\,,\quad\hbox{and}\quad{\rm div}(\eta_{e}\mathbf{v}_{e})=0\,. (4.1)

Consequently, at equilibrium the gradients ∇ℬ~e\nabla\tilde{\cal B}_{e} and ∇qe\nabla q_{e} are collinear because they are both orthogonal in the ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} plane to 𝐯e\mathbf{v}_{e}. A sufficient condition for this collinearity is a functional relationship which we choose to write as

ℬ~​(𝐮e,ηe)=qe​Φ′​(qe)−Φ⁡(qe),\displaystyle\tilde{\cal B}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e})=q_{e}\Phi^{\prime}(q_{e})-\Phi(q_{e})\,, (4.2)

for some twice differentiable function Φ⁡(ξ)\Phi(\xi), with ξ∈ℝ\xi\in\mathbb{R}, defined wherever ∇qe\nabla q_{e} does not vanish.

Applying the operator qe−1𝐳^×q_{e}^{-1}\mathbf{\widehat{z}}\times to the first equilibrium condition in equation (4.1) and using relation (4.2) yields

ηe​𝐯e=qe−1​𝐳^×∇ℬ~​(𝐮e,ηe)=qe−1​𝐳^×∇(qe​Φ′​(qe)−Φ⁡(qe))=𝐳^×∇Φ′​(qe),\displaystyle\eta_{e}\mathbf{v}_{e}=q_{e}^{-1}\mathbf{\widehat{z}}\times\nabla\tilde{\cal B}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e})=q_{e}^{-1}\mathbf{\widehat{z}}\times\nabla\big(q_{e}\Phi^{\prime}(q_{e})-\Phi(q_{e})\big)=\mathbf{\widehat{z}}\times\nabla\Phi^{\prime}(q_{e})\,, (4.3)

which also implies the last equilibrium condition in equation (4.1); namely, div⁡(ηe​𝐯e)=0{\rm div}(\eta_{e}\mathbf{v}_{e})=0.

The 1s​t1^{st} variation of hΦ​(𝐮,η)h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u},\eta)

Proposition 4.1.

Critical points of the sum of the 2D BKBK Hamiltonian and its Lie–Poisson Casimirs given by

hΦ​(𝐮,η):=h⁡(𝐮,η)+CΦ:=∫ℝ2η​|𝐮|22−κ​𝐮⋅∇η+12​η2+η​Φ​(q)​d2​x,\displaystyle\begin{split}h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u},\eta):=h(\mathbf{u},\eta)+C_{\Phi}:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\eta\frac{|\mathbf{u}|^{2}}{2}-\kappa\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\eta+\frac{1}{2}\eta^{2}+\eta\Phi(q)\,d^{2}x\,,\end{split} (4.4)

are equilibrium solutions of the 2D BKBK system in (3.13).

Proof.

Upon using the definition q:=η−1​𝐳^⋅curl​𝐮q:=\eta^{-1}\mathbf{\hat{z}}\cdot{\rm curl}\,\mathbf{u} in (3.11) to obtain the variational relation

δ​q=−η−1​q​δ​η+η−1​𝐳^⋅curl​δ​𝐮,\displaystyle\delta q=-\,\eta^{-1}q\,\delta\eta+\eta^{-1}\mathbf{\hat{z}}\cdot{\rm curl}\,\delta\mathbf{u}\,, (4.5)

and assuming that the velocity variation δ​𝐮\delta\mathbf{u} vanishes at spatial infinity of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} (or has zero circulation on any boundary which may be present in an enclosed flow domain 𝒟{\cal D}), then one finds that critical points of hΦ​(𝐮,η)h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u},\eta) in (2.5) satisfy the following equations,

0=δ​hΦ​(𝐮,η)=⟨η𝐮−κ∇η−𝐳^×∇Φ′(q),δ𝐮⟩+⟨12​|𝐮|2+κ​div​(𝐮)+η+Φ⁡(q)−q​Φ′​(q),δ​η⟩=⟨η​𝐯−𝐳^×∇Φ′​(q),δ​𝐮⟩+⟨ℬ~​(𝐮,η)+Φ⁡(q)−q​Φ′​(q),δ​η⟩,\displaystyle\begin{split}0=\delta h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u},\eta)&={\left\langle{\eta\mathbf{u}-\kappa\,\nabla\eta-\mathbf{\hat{z}}\times\nabla\Phi^{\prime}(q)}\,,\,{\delta\mathbf{u}}\right\rangle}\\ &\quad+{\left\langle{\tfrac{1}{2}|\mathbf{u}|^{2}+{\kappa}{\rm div}(\mathbf{u})+\eta+\Phi(q)-q\Phi^{\prime}(q)}\,,\,{\delta\eta}\right\rangle}\\ &={\left\langle{\eta\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{\hat{z}}\times\nabla\Phi^{\prime}(q)}\,,\,{\delta\mathbf{u}}\right\rangle}+{\left\langle{\tilde{\cal B}(\mathbf{u},\eta)+\Phi(q)-q\Phi^{\prime}(q)}\,,\,{\delta\eta}\right\rangle}\,,\end{split} (4.6)

in which the angle brackets ⟨⋅,⋅⟩{\left\langle{\,\cdot\,}\,,\,{\,\cdot\,}\right\rangle} denote L2L^{2} pairing on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} (or an enclosed flow domain 𝒟{\cal D}). ∎

Thus, critical points of hΦ​(𝐮,η)h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u},\eta) in (2.5) are equilibrium solutions of the 2D BKBK equations in (3.13). These critical points satisfy the conditions

ηe​𝐯e−𝐳^×∇Φ′​(qe)=0and12​|𝐮e|2+κ​div​(𝐮e)+ηe+Φ⁡(qe)−qe​Φ′​(qe)=0,\displaystyle\eta_{e}\mathbf{v}_{e}-\mathbf{\hat{z}}\times\nabla\Phi^{\prime}(q_{e})=0\quad\hbox{and}\quad\tfrac{1}{2}|\mathbf{u}_{e}|^{2}+\kappa{\rm div}(\mathbf{u}_{e})+\eta_{e}+\Phi(q_{e})-q_{e}\Phi^{\prime}(q_{e})=0\,, (4.7)

for any choice of the functions Φ⁡(q)\Phi(q) of potential vorticity qq in (3.16). Consequently, the twice-differentiable functions Φ⁡(q)\Phi(q) provide a class of equilibrium solutions of the 2D BKBK system in (3.13).

The 2nd variation of hΦ​(𝐮,η)h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u},\eta)

Upon recalling the definitions of ℬ~\tilde{\cal B} in (3.14) and 𝐯\mathbf{v} in (3.1),

ℬ~(𝐮,η):=12|𝐮|2+gη+κdiv(𝐮)and𝐯:=𝐮−κ∇lnη,\displaystyle\tilde{\cal B}(\mathbf{u},\eta):=\tfrac{1}{2}|\mathbf{u}|^{2}+g\eta+\kappa{\rm div}(\mathbf{u})\quad\hbox{and}\quad\mathbf{v}:=\mathbf{u}-\kappa\nabla\ln\eta\,, (4.8)

one may rewrite the variation δ​hΦ​(𝐮,η)\delta h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u},\eta) in (4.6) to separate its κ\kappa terms as

δ​hΦ​(𝐮,η)=⟨η​𝐮−𝐳^×∇Φ′​(q),δ​𝐮⟩+⟨12​|𝐮|2+η+Φ⁡(q)−q​Φ′​(q),δ​η⟩+κ​⟨div⁡(𝐮),δ​η⟩.\displaystyle\begin{split}\delta h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u},\eta)&={\left\langle{\eta\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{\hat{z}}\times\nabla\Phi^{\prime}(q)}\,,\,{\delta\mathbf{u}}\right\rangle}\\ &\quad+{\left\langle{\tfrac{1}{2}|\mathbf{u}|^{2}+\eta+\Phi(q)-q\Phi^{\prime}(q)}\,,\,{\delta\eta}\right\rangle}\\ &\quad+\kappa{\left\langle{{\rm div}(\mathbf{u})}\,,\,{\delta\eta}\right\rangle}\,.\end{split} (4.9)

One may then calculate the second variation δ2​hΦ​(𝐮e,ηe)\delta^{2}h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e}) which is in fact the conserved energy for the linearised dynamics of perturbations of the BKBK equilibria arising as critical points of hΦ​(𝐮e,ηe)h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e}) in (2.5). The calculation of the second variation δ2​hΦ​(𝐮e,ηe)\delta^{2}h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e}) then yields

δ2​hΦ​(𝐮e,ηe)=∫ℝ22​δ​η​δ​𝐮⋅𝐮e+ηe​(δ​𝐮)2+(δ​η)2−2​κ​δ​𝐮⋅δ⁡(∇η)+ηe​Φ′′​(qe)​(δ​q)2​d2​x.\displaystyle\begin{split}\delta^{2}h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}2\delta\eta\,\delta\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u}_{e}+\eta_{e}(\delta\mathbf{u})^{2}+(\delta\eta)^{2}-2\kappa\delta\mathbf{u}\cdot\delta(\nabla\eta)+\eta_{e}\Phi^{\prime\prime}(q_{e})(\delta q)^{2}\,d^{2}x\,.\end{split} (4.10)

By treating δ​η\delta\eta and δ∇η\delta\nabla\eta as independent variables, one may organise δ2​hΦ​(𝐮e,ηe)\delta^{2}h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e}) as

δ2​hΦ​(𝐮e,ηe)\displaystyle\delta^{2}h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e}) =∫ℝ[δ​𝐮δ​ηδ∇η]T​[ηeue−κue10−κ00]​[δ​𝐮δ​ηδ∇η]+ηe​Φ′′​(qe)​(δ​q)2​d2​x.\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\begin{bmatrix}\delta\mathbf{u}\\ \delta\eta\\ \delta\nabla\eta\end{bmatrix}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}\eta_{e}&u_{e}&-\kappa\\ u_{e}&1&0\\ -\kappa&0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\delta\mathbf{u}\\ \delta\eta\\ \delta\nabla\eta\end{bmatrix}+\eta_{e}\Phi^{\prime\prime}(q_{e})(\delta q)^{2}d^{2}x\,. (4.11)

The linear stability of the 2D BKBK equilibrium solutions in the class δ​hΦ​(𝐮e,ηe)=0\delta h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e})=0 requires the symmetric operator in (4.11) to be positive definite. Via direct calculation, the determinant of the symmetric operator, det⁡(δ2​hΦ)=−κ2<0\operatorname{\det}(\delta^{2}h_{\Phi})=-\kappa^{2}<0 such that the linear Lyapunov stability conditions is not satisfied. Enforcing the condition δ(∇η)=∇δη\delta(\nabla\eta)=\nabla\delta\eta, the extent to which linear Lyapunov stability condition is not satisfied is revealed by re-organising δ2​hΦ​(𝐮e,ηe)\delta^{2}h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e}) as

δ2​hΦ​(𝐮e,ηe)=∫ℝ[δ​𝐮δ​η]T​[ηeue−κ∇ue+κ∇⋅1]​[δ​𝐮δ​η]+ηe​Φ′′​(qe)​(δ​q)2​d2​x.\displaystyle\begin{split}\delta^{2}h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e})&=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\begin{bmatrix}\delta\mathbf{u}\\ \delta\eta\end{bmatrix}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}\eta_{e}&u_{e}-\kappa\nabla\\ u_{e}+\kappa\nabla\cdot&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\delta\mathbf{u}\\ \delta\eta\end{bmatrix}+\eta_{e}\Phi^{\prime\prime}(q_{e})(\delta q)^{2}d^{2}x\,.\end{split} (4.12)

For the case of shallow water dynamics arising for κ=0\kappa=0, requiring definiteness in sign of δ2​hΦ​(𝐮e,ηe)\delta^{2}h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e}) provides sufficient conditions for linear Lyapunov stability of 2D shallow water equilibrium solutions that are obtained from setting δ​hΦ​(𝐮e,ηe)=0\delta h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e})=0 with κ=0\kappa=0. This was shown for similar equations for barotropic ideal compressible fluid dynamics in [HMRW83, HMRW85]. For the singular perturbation of nonzero κ\kappa, though, linear stability of perturbed 2D BKBK equilibrium solutions in the class δ​hΦ​(𝐮e,ηe)=0\delta h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e})=0 require in addition that the spectrum of the symmetric elliptic operator in (4.12) be positive definite. The symbol of the elliptic operator in (4.12) is of the form

σ⁡(|𝐤|2)≈ηe−(𝐮e2+κ2​|𝐤|2),\displaystyle\sigma(|\mathbf{k}|^{2})\approx\eta_{e}-\big(\mathbf{u}_{e}^{2}+\kappa^{2}\,|\mathbf{k}|^{2}\big)\,, (4.13)

in which the equilibrium solutions ηe\eta_{e} and 𝐮e\mathbf{u}_{e} satisfy ηe​(𝐱)−𝐮e​(𝐱)2>0{\eta}_{e}(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{{u}}_{e}(\mathbf{x})^{2}>0. Hence, the linear Lyapunov stability conditions obtained from requiring positivity of the second variation of the Hamiltonian δ2​hΦ​(𝐮e,ηe)\delta^{2}h_{\Phi}(\mathbf{u}_{e},\eta_{e}) in (4.12) cannot hold for arbitrarily high wavenumber magnitudes |𝐤||\mathbf{k}|.

5 Simulations of solution behaviour for the BKBK equations

This section investigates computational simulations of the BKBK system in 1D and 2D. In the 1D simulations of the BKBK system (1.4), high-wavenumber instabilities are controlled here by introducing 4th-order dissipation in both velocity and elevation, reminiscent of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation. Computational simulations are then used to investigate the travelling wave solution and nonlinear wave interactions of initially Gaussian wave elevations. In the 2D simulations of the BKBK system (3.3), we employ a Hamiltonian regularisation where the 2D BKBK Hamiltonian (3.9) is augmented to include an energy penalty for wave height gradients. Using the regularised BKBK equations (5.6), we investigate the interaction of waves with and without potential vorticity, for both signs of κ\kappa.

5.1 1D BKBK system simulation

As discussed upon introducing the 1D BKBK system in section 1.1, the dispersion relation for BKBK in equation (1.5) indicates high-wavenumber instability. Direct simulation for (1.4) is unstable even for analytical travelling solutions. This is reminiscent of the similar negative diffusion situation in the well-known Kuramoto-Shivashinski equation in 1D,

ut+u​ux+ux​x+ux​x​x​x=0.\displaystyle u_{t}+uu_{x}+u_{xx}+u_{xxxx}=0\,. (5.1)

For periodic boundary conditions, we introduce the following 4th-order dissipation term into the motion equation of the BKBK 1D system (1.4) as,

ut=−(u2/2+η+κ​ux+ν​ux​x​x)x,ηt=−(u​η−κ​ηx+ν​ηx​x​x)x.\displaystyle\begin{split}{u}_{t}&=-\left({u}^{2}/2+{\eta}+\kappa{u}_{x}+\nu u_{xxx}\right)_{x}\,,\\ {\eta}_{t}&=-\left({u}{\eta}-\kappa{\eta}_{x}+\nu\eta_{xxx}\right)_{x}\,.\end{split} (5.2)

When the fourth-order dissipation coefficients are unequal, νu≠νη\nu_{u}\neq\nu_{\eta}, the dispersion relation acquires a k6k^{6} cross term proportional to κ⁡(νu−νη)​k6\kappa\left(\nu_{u}-\nu_{\eta}\right)k^{6} in the quadratic form for −i​ω-i\omega. This term couples phase and damping and can create a finite band of unstable wavenumbers even when both νu,νη>0\nu_{u},\nu_{\eta}>0. The symmetric choice of ν\nu as in (5.2) leads to the following dispersion relation

ω/k=−i​ν​k3±g​η0−κ2​k2,withg​η0=1,\omega/k=-i\nu k^{3}\pm\sqrt{g\eta_{0}-\kappa^{2}k^{2}}\,,\quad\hbox{with}\quad g\eta_{0}=1\,,

which is the same as (1.5) with an additional pure damping term and two dimension-free numbers g​η0/(k​κ)2g\eta_{0}/(k\kappa)^{2} and k2​ν/κk^{2}\nu/\kappa. Here the terms k​κk\kappa, g​η0\sqrt{g\eta_{0}}, ν​k3\nu k^{3}, ω/k\omega/k all have the units of velocity, [u]=[L]/[T][u]=[L]/[T]. For wavenumbers |k|>kc=g​η0/|κ||k|>k_{c}=\sqrt{g\eta_{0}}/|\kappa|, choosing ν>νc​r=2​|κ|33​3​g​η0\nu>\nu_{cr}=\frac{2|\kappa|^{3}}{3\sqrt{3}g\eta_{0}} is necessary to ensure the growth rate satisfies Im⁡ω⁡(k)<0\operatorname{Im}\omega(k)<0 for all kk, thereby eliminating the unstable band of modes.

We use the nonsingular travelling wave (5.3) as a benchmark initial condition (figure 1(a)), as reported in [XYZ01].

u⁡(x,t)=c−λ​|κ|​tanh⁡(λ2​(x−c​t+ϕ)),η⁡(x,t)=λ22​|κ|​(|κ|+κ)​sech2⁡(λ2​(x−c​t+ϕ)),\begin{split}u(x,t)&=c-\lambda|\kappa|\tanh\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}(x-ct+\phi)\right)\,,\\ \eta(x,t)&=\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}|\kappa|(|\kappa|+\kappa)\operatorname{sech}^{2}\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}(x-ct+\phi)\right)\,,\end{split} (5.3)

where λ,c,ϕ\lambda,c,\phi are constants. Although it is an exact solution of the unregularized BKBK system, direct time stepping of (1.4) is numerically unstable. The symmetric regularisation (5.2) provides a controlled setting for assessing (i) preservation of the wave profile at low wavenumbers, (ii) suppression of high-kk growth, and (iii) the dependence of phase speed and spectral energy transfer on dissipation.

5.2 2D BKBK system simulation

In the computational simulations of the two-dimensional BKBK system (3.3), we find that no fourth-order dissipation is required. Instead, we use a modified BKBK system derived from a regularised Hamiltonian constructed by augmenting the BKBK Hamiltonian (3.14) to include an energy penalty for large wave slope as presented in [Hol25]. Namely,

h⁡(m,η)=∫M|𝐦|22​η−κ​𝐦⋅∇ln⁡(η)+12​(η2+α2​|∇η|2)​d2​x,h(m,\eta)=\int_{M}\frac{|\mathbf{m}|^{2}}{2\eta}-\kappa\mathbf{m}\cdot\nabla\ln(\eta)+\frac{1}{2}\left(\eta^{2}+\alpha^{2}|\nabla\eta|^{2}\right)d^{2}x\,, (5.4)

whose variational derivatives are given by

δ​hδ​𝐦=𝐦/η−κ∇ln(η)=𝐮−κ∇ln(η)=:𝐯,δ​hδ​η=−|𝐦|22​η2+κη​div⁡𝐦+g⁡(1−α2​Δ)​η=:−ℬ.\displaystyle\begin{split}\frac{\delta h}{\delta\mathbf{m}}&=\mathbf{m}/\eta-\kappa\nabla\ln(\eta)=\mathbf{u}-\kappa\nabla\ln(\eta)=:\mathbf{v},\\ \frac{\delta h}{\delta\eta}&=-\frac{|\mathbf{m}|^{2}}{2\eta^{2}}+\frac{\kappa}{\eta}\operatorname{div}\mathbf{m}+\mathrm{g}\left(1-\alpha^{2}\Delta\right)\eta=:-{\cal B}\,.\end{split} (5.5)

The regularised Hamiltonian (5.4) mimics the Hamiltonian formulation of the Lagrangian Averaged Navier Stokes α\alpha (LANS-α\alpha) subgrid scale model [CFH+98] in which the gradient energy penalty is on the velocity uu, rather than the height η\eta. This energy penalty introduces nonlinear dispersion, which suppresses high-wavenumber activity without artificial viscosity, thereby preserving the conservative/geometric structure (energy, Kelvin circulation, and potential-vorticity conservation in the classic shallow water model). As shown below in the results of numerical simulations, coherent vortical features remain sharp and the high-wavenumber blow-up seen in 1D is controlled.

After transforming from the Lie–Poisson operator form (2.16) the regularised 2D BKBK system may be expressed in fluid dynamics notation as

∂t𝐮+(𝐯⋅∇)𝐮+uj∇vj=∇ℬ,∂tη+div(η𝐯)=0,𝐯:=𝐮−κ∇ln(η).\displaystyle\begin{split}\partial_{t}\mathbf{u}&+(\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{u}+u_{j}\nabla v^{j}=\nabla{\cal B},\\ \partial_{t}\eta&+\operatorname{div}(\eta\mathbf{v})=0,\qquad\mathbf{v}:=\mathbf{u}-\kappa\nabla\ln(\eta)\,.\end{split} (5.6)

The 2D BKBK system (5.6) represents shallow water dynamics with modified transport velocity 𝐯\mathbf{v} and Bernoulli function B⁡(𝐮,η)B(\mathbf{u},\eta) defined in (5.5). The remainder of this section provides examples of their solution behaviour. Section 4 reprises their variational derivation.

We solve the two-dimensional shallow water equations using the pseudo-spectral method in a periodic domain of size Lx×Ly=16×16L_{x}\times L_{y}=16\times 16 with resolution 192×192192\times 192. Time integration uses the semi-implicit SBDF2 scheme with a timestep 10−610^{-6}, up to a final time t=2.0t=2.0. Model parameters are g=1,α=0.02g=1,\alpha=0.02, κ=−0.5\kappa=-0.5, and κ=−0.05\kappa=-0.05. The background depth is η0=4.0\eta_{0}=4.0 with no mean flow. The initial free-surface height is given by two positive Gaussian ridges of amplitude h0=4.0h_{0}=4.0 (width σ=0.7\sigma=0.7 ) centered at (x,y)=(Lx/2±δ​x,0)(x,y)=\left(L_{x}/2\pm\delta x,0\right), with δ​x=1.1​σ\delta x=1.1\sigma, together with two weaker negative Gaussian anomalies of amplitude −0.01​h0-0.01h_{0} at (x,y)=(Lx/2,±δ​y)(x,y)=\left(L_{x}/2,\pm\delta y\right), with δ​y=1.7​σ\delta y=1.7\sigma. The velocity field is initialized in geostrophic balance u=−g𝐳^×∇η/f0u=-g\hat{\mathbf{z}}\times\nabla\eta/f_{0} with f0=50f_{0}=50.

We solve the two-dimensional shallow water equations in a periodic domain of size Lx×Ly=24×16L_{x}\times L_{y}=24\times 16, discretized with 384×256384\times 256 grid points. The initial condition is a localized perturbation of velocity in the xx component, given by ux(x,y)=W(−8/3,8/3;0.5;y)W(10,11;0.5;x)u_{x}(x,y)=W(-8/3,8/3;0.5;y)W(10,11;0.5;x) where W⁡(a,b,δ,z)=12​[tanh⁡(z−aδ)−tanh⁡(z−bδ)]W(a,b;\delta;z)=\frac{1}{2}\left[\tanh\left(\frac{z-a}{\delta}\right)-\tanh\left(\frac{z-b}{\delta}\right)\right] is a smooth rectangular window. Other parameters and numerical settings are the same as in the previous experiments.

6 Summary conclusion and open questions

One of the first observations in this paper is that the BKBK system introduces a dynamical shift in the transport velocity in the motion equations and the advection equations in both the 1D and 2D BKBK systems. This dynamical shift in the transport velocity is proportional to the real constant κ\kappa, and when κ=0\kappa=0 one formally recovers the classical shallow water wave equations. See, e.g., equation (1.4).

However, the BKBK shift in transport velocity comprises a singular perturbation which also introduces backwards diffusion in the motion equation. As shown in equation (1.5) for 1D BKBK, this feature produces high-wavenumber instabilities whose exponential growth rates increase as ω⁡(k)=±i​k​1−κ2​k2\omega(k)=\pm ik\sqrt{1-\kappa^{2}k^{2}}. Thus, although the 1D BKBK system is known to be completely integrable [Kau75, Kup85], its solution behaviour is ill-posed for real values of κ\kappa. One notices, though, that this high-wavenumber instability would not occur if the parameter κ\kappa were imaginary, instead of being real.

Section 2 reframes the 1D BKBK system as a Lie–Poisson Hamiltonian system and then explores its relation with modulation instability [Per83], by noticing that the Madelung transformation transforms the BKBK Hamiltonian in (2.11) into the Hamiltonian for the focusing NLS equation. Given this observation, studies of instability of water waves using the 1D BKBK system with real κ\kappa may be regarded as being complementary to the traditional study of modulation instability of water waves using the 1D NLS equation as in [Per83].

In preparation for developing ideas for regularisation of the BKBK system to help meet the challenges of its computational simulations, section 3 explains the variational derivations of the 2D BKBK system, as well as its Hamiltonian structures and their implications such as the Lagrangian advection of potential vorticity and its associated conservation laws.

Section 4 uses the Hamiltonian structures investigated in section 3 to develop a classification of the equilibrium solutions of the 2D BKBK system and to determine the conditions for the linear Lyapunov stability of these equilibria by using the energy-Casimir approach [HMRW85]. The Lyapunov stability conditions obtained from the energy-Casimir approach extend the class of 2D BKBK equilibria to finite velocity and match the instability results obtained by linearising the BKBK equations around equilibria with vanishing velocity and constant elevation.

In section 5, the figures for the computational simulations of the regularised 1D BKBK system (5.2) show that introducing fourth-order dissipation with coefficient 0<ν≪10<\nu\ll 1 prevents the ill-posed growth observed in the 1D BKBK unregularised system with ν=0\nu=0. This regularisation of the 1D BKBK system by introducing fourth-order dissipation has the advantage that it may also introduce a new variant of the Kuramoto–Shivashinsky equation [CH93] which may have interesting low dimensional solution behaviour for 1D BKBK shallow water wave dynamics, although this investigation would be for future research.

In 2D, the BKBK transport velocity shift also appears in the material loop velocity in the 2D Kelvin circulation theorem as well as in the transport of the potential vorticity, as discussed in section 4. In studying 2D computational simulations of the BKBK system (5.6) in section 5, we used a regularised Hamiltonian accomplished by augmenting the 2D BKBK Hamiltonian to include an energy penalty for large wave slope. See equation (5.4).

Section 5 shows the first simulations of the regularised BKBK dynamics derived here in both 1D and 2D. These simulations represent proof of principle and indication of interesting dynamics of the regularised BKBK flows. Further investigations of the sensitivity of the solutions to the magnitude and sign of κ\kappa, for example, are deferred for future research.
